pages.text: Friday was the Career Technology Enterprise Fair, and Group B planned to sell eighty meat pies and eighty cups of chilled sobolo. In the food laboratory, Serwaa put hygiene first. Hair went under clean caps. Fingernails were short. Hands were washed with soap. Raw minced beef stayed on its own board, away from the washed vegetables, to prevent cross-contamination. Then she turned to the recipe. Their test batch had made twenty pies, so for eighty she needed four times as much: a ratio of 1 : 4. She multiplied every gram of flour, margarine, and beef by four, so that each pie would be the same.
sentences: Friday was the Career Technology Enterprise Fair, and Group B planned to sell eighty meat pies and eighty cups of chilled sobolo.
In the food laboratory, Serwaa put hygiene first.
Hair went under clean caps.
Fingernails were short.
Hands were washed with soap.
Raw minced beef stayed on its own board, away from the washed vegetables, to prevent cross-contamination.
Then she turned to the recipe.
Their test batch had made twenty pies, so for eighty she needed four times as much: a ratio of 1 : 4.
She multiplied every gram of flour, margarine, and beef by four, so that each pie would be the same.
pages.alt: Inside a spotless Ghanaian JHS food laboratory, Serwaa and Latifa in white aprons and hairnets weigh flour on digital scales while keeping raw meat on a separate chopping board.

pages.text: Next door in the ICT laboratory, Nii opened a spreadsheet for the budget. Flour went in row 2, margarine in row 3, minced beef in row 4, and charcoal and packaging in row 5. Column B held the quantity, column C the unit price, and column D the subtotal. Nii worked out 5 × 12 in his head and typed 60 into cell D2. Then the price of flour rose from GH¢ 12 to GH¢ 14 a kilogram. He changed C2, but his totals did not move. Latifa saw why. “You typed a plain number. A formula must begin with an equals sign and use cell references. Type =B2*C2 in D2, and =SUM(D2:D5) in D6. Then the sheet recalculates whenever a price changes.”

Flour went in row 2, margarine in row 3, minced beef in row 4, and charcoal and packaging in row 5.
Column B held the quantity, column C the unit price, and column D the subtotal.
Nii worked out 5 × 12 in his head and typed 60 into cell D2.
Then the price of flour rose from GH¢ 12 to GH¢ 14 a kilogram.
He changed C2, but his totals did not move.
Latifa saw why.
“You typed a plain number.
A formula must begin with an equals sign and use cell references.
Type =B2*C2 in D2, and =SUM(D2:D5) in D6.
Then the sheet recalculates whenever a price changes.”
pages.alt: Close-up gouache view of a computer monitor showing a neat spreadsheet grid (Columns A to D, Rows 1 to 6) with =B2*C2 highlighted in D2 and =SUM(D2:D5) in cell D6.

pages.text: With the new prices, cell D6 showed a total cost price of GH¢ 320.00 for the eighty pies. (The sobolo had its own budget.) So each pie cost GH¢ 4.00 to make. “Let us sell at GH¢ 5.00,” said Nii. “Eighty pies bring in GH¢ 400. That is GH¢ 80 profit. And 80 divided by 400 is 20% profit!” Latifa opened her Mathematics notebook. “Careful, Nii. That is a common BECE mistake. Percentage profit is worked out on the cost price. Divide the GH¢ 80 profit by the GH¢ 320 cost price and multiply by 100. You get 25%. Dividing by the GH¢ 400 selling price gives something different: a 20% margin on sales.”
sentences: With the new prices, cell D6 showed a total cost price of GH¢ 320.00 for the eighty pies.
(The sobolo had its own budget.) So each pie cost GH¢ 4.00 to make.
“Let us sell at GH¢ 5.00,” said Nii.
“Eighty pies bring in GH¢ 400.
That is GH¢ 80 profit.
And 80 divided by 400 is 20% profit!” Latifa opened her Mathematics notebook.
“Careful, Nii.
That is a common BECE mistake.
Percentage profit is worked out on the cost price.
Divide the GH¢ 80 profit by the GH¢ 320 cost price and multiply by 100.
You get 25%.
Dividing by the GH¢ 400 selling price gives something different: a 20% margin on sales.”
pages.alt: Latifa points to a whiteboard comparison showing Percentage Profit = (Profit / Cost Price) x 100% = (80 / 320) x 100% = 25%, crossing out division by Selling Price.

pages.text: Madam Osei praised the correction. Then she asked a harder question. “Suppose rain keeps customers away. How many pies must you sell at GH¢ 5.00 just to get your GH¢ 320.00 back?” Serwaa wrote a linear equation on the board. Let x be the number of pies sold. Then 5x = 320, so x = 320 ÷ 5 = 64. “Sixty-four pies is our break-even point,” she explained. “At that point our sales equal the cost price of all eighty pies, so there is no profit and no loss. Real profit starts with pie number sixty-five.”

pages.alt: Serwaa writing the linear equation 5x = 320 -> x = 64 pies on the classroom board beside a colourful spreadsheet column chart comparing Cost Price and Revenue.

pages.text: Before printing price tags, Nii wanted the sheet to work out the selling price by itself: the cost price plus 25%, shared among eighty pies. He typed =D6+D6*0.25/80 into cell E6. The answer was 321. “GH¢ 321 for one pie?” Serwaa laughed. Nii frowned, then remembered operator precedence. A spreadsheet multiplies and divides before it adds, unless brackets say otherwise. He typed =(D6+D6*0.25)/80, and E6 showed 5.00. He also made a bar chart of the costs. It showed that minced beef took 45% of the budget, while charcoal and packaging took only 10%.
sentences: Before printing price tags, Nii wanted the sheet to work out the selling price by itself: the cost price plus 25%, shared among eighty pies.
He typed =D6+D6*0.25/80 into cell E6.
The answer was 321.
“GH¢ 321 for one pie?” Serwaa laughed.
Nii frowned, then remembered operator precedence.
A spreadsheet multiplies and divides before it adds, unless brackets say otherwise.
He typed =(D6+D6*0.25)/80, and E6 showed 5.00.
He also made a bar chart of the costs.
It showed that minced beef took 45% of the budget, while charcoal and packaging took only 10%.
pages.alt: Nii and Serwaa reviewing a printed cost-breakdown bar chart and neat price tags produced in the JHS computer lab.

pages.text: On Friday afternoon, customers queued at Group B’s covered glass showcase. The pies were all the same size. The sobolo was chilled on clean ice. Every sale was recorded against the spreadsheet budget. By 2:00 p.m., all eighty pies were gone. Latifa counted GH¢ 400.00 from the pies. The group set aside GH¢ 320.00 to replace what the pies had cost. That left GH¢ 80.00 profit for the club’s next project. Clean food, a spreadsheet that recalculated by itself, and careful mathematics had turned a classroom recipe into a real business.

activities.question: Why is typing =B2*C2 in cell D2 better than typing =5*12 or 60?
options: Spreadsheets refuse to display numbers unless letters are typed in every cell
Subtotals and SUM update automatically when quantity or price changes
Typing 120 deletes all rows above row 2 permanently

activities.question: A student group spends GH¢ 320.00 (Cost Price) making snacks and sells them all for GH¢ 400.00 (Selling Price). What is their exact percentage profit?
options: 20%, because Profit (GH¢ 80) is divided by Selling Price (GH¢ 400)
25%, because Profit (GH¢ 80) is divided by Cost Price (GH¢ 320)

activities.question: Using standard spreadsheet operator precedence, what value will the formula =10+6*2 display in a cell?
options: 22, because multiplication (6 * 2 = 12) is performed before addition (10 + 12)
32, because calculation is evaluated strictly left to right

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the enterprise project in the correct order.
items: Wash hands, wear caps, and scale the 20-pie recipe up in ratio 1 : 4.
Enter ingredient quantities and prices into a spreadsheet with =B2*C2 and =SUM.
Find cost per pie, solve break-even 5x = 320, and check 25% profit.
Sell the covered pies, set aside the GH¢ 320 cost, and record the GH¢ 80 profit.
